frames.narration: Account acct-7 starts at balance 0. The producer sends two events: deposit 100 (v1) then withdraw 60 (v2). With no key, the topic spreads messages round-robin: v1 lands on partition 0, v2 on partition 1.

Each consumer owns its own partition and runs in parallel. Consumer B is idle and takes v2 first, while A is still busy with an older message. The withdrawal hits balance 0 and fails: an overdraft that never happened in real life.

Parallelism and global order do not mix. The fix is a message key: the producer hashes the account id (FNV-1a or murmur2) modulo the partition count. hash(acct-7) mod 2 = 0, so every acct-7 event goes to partition 0, in send order.

A partition is read by exactly one consumer in the group, in offset order. Consumer A applies v1 (balance 100) and then v2 (balance 40). Order within the account is guaranteed; no order is promised between different accounts.

The price: parallelism is capped by the partition count, and a hot account stays on one partition. If acct-1 sends 90% of the traffic, partition 0 and consumer A are saturated while B sits idle, and adding a third consumer would not help.

Retries can break order even with a key. Withdraw v2 fails (a downstream timeout) and is sent to a retry topic. Meanwhile deposit v3 (20) is applied, then v2 returns after it. Blocking the partition and retrying v2 in place avoids this, at the cost of delaying everything behind it.

A consumer can also tolerate disorder by itself. Events carry a version; the consumer keeps the stored version (here 1) and applies only version 2 next. v3 arrives early, so it is held back until v2 shows up (gap detection), then both apply in order.

Resizing is dangerous: going from 2 to 3 partitions changes hash(acct-7) mod n from 0 to 1. A new event goes to partition 1 and a free consumer applies it while the old acct-7 events are still queued on partition 0. Drain first, or pause the key, before you change the count.
